analysis.one_liner: Speeds cheaper generic drugs to market by curbing brand-name drug makers' patent delay tactics.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan generic-drug bill with 31 cosponsors was referred to a House committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it easier and faster for generic versions of brand-name drugs to reach the market. It tightened the rules brand-name companies use to list patents, limited the 30-month hold on generic approvals that patent lawsuits trigger, and stripped the 180-day exclusivity reward from generic companies that sit on their approvals. Congressional findings in the bill itself cite estimates that generics cost 25 to 60 percent less per prescription, with total savings of $8 to $10 billion a year for purchasers.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy prescription drugs — especially seniors and people without insurance — would have gained from earlier generic competition and lower prices. Generic drug manufacturers would have gained faster market entry. The bill's own findings cite Congressional Budget Office estimates of $8-10 billion in annual savings and per-prescription savings of $15-30 [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires brand-name companies to register drug patents with the FDA within 30 days; a patent not registered on time could not be used to sue generic competitors [S2].
Blocks extensions of the 30-month stay of generic approval for patents issued after a drug is approved, closing a tactic that could delay generic entry repeatedly [S2].

Strips the 180-day generic exclusivity period from a first generic applicant that delays or prevents its own drug from reaching the market — targeting arrangements where a generic company is paid to stay out [S2].
Bars patent suits filed too late (more than 45 days after notice), so generic approvals cannot be held up indefinitely by last-minute litigation [S2].
The bill's findings cite CBO estimates that generic substitution could save purchasers $8-10 billion per year, with generics costing 25-60 percent less than brand-name drugs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies, which would face earlier generic competition, fewer tools to delay generic approvals through patent litigation, and loss of the patent-infringement suits available when patents were not registered on time [S2]. To the extent weaker patent enforcement reduces returns on drug development, some future innovation incentives could be affected as well.

drawbacks.text: Limiting the 30-month stay and barring late patent suits weakens the patent enforcement brand-name companies rely on, and the bill itself includes 'fair treatment for innovators' provisions — confidential disclosure of generic applicants' formulations and a rule that courts may not deny injunctions based on a generic company's ability to pay damages — showing lawmakers recognized the bill tilted against patent holders [S3].

Forfeiting the 180-day exclusivity for delay removes a reward that has encouraged generic companies to challenge weak patents; removing or reshaping that incentive could mean fewer patent challenges and slower generic entry in some cases [S2].

Pushing courts to expedite infringement cases and restricting consideration of an applicant's ability to pay damages shifts significant discretion from judges to a statutory formula, which may produce blunt outcomes in complex patent disputes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer upside was large and well-documented: generics at 25-60 percent less, with multi-billion-dollar annual savings cited in the bill's own findings [S3]. The main cost falls on brand-name drug makers' patent enforcement, and there is a real but harder-to-quantify risk to drug innovation incentives. On balance the bill was designed to shift the balance toward generic competition, with explicit compromises to protect innovators' litigation rights.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health subcommittee, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. John Thune (R-SD) introduced the Prescription Drug Affordability Act on July 26, 2002, with 10 original cosponsors [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on July 26, 2002 [S5].
On July 29, 2002, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill attracted 31 cosponsors across party lines — 21 Republicans, 9 Democrats, and 1 Independent — but no committee action followed [S4].
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill died without ever reaching the House floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, whose patent listing and litigation tools remained unchanged, and the generic-drug status quo, since no reform of the 180-day exclusivity or 30-month stay occurred in that Congress.

for.name: Rep. John Thune
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Prescription Drug Affordability Act on July 26, 2002

for.name: 31 House cosponsors (21 of 223 Republicans, 9 of 208 Democrats, 1 of 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (Chair, Rep. Billy Tauzin)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out; after referral to the Health subcommittee, no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan — 21 Republicans, 9 Democrats, and 1 Independent signed on — and its death was not a recorded party vote but the absence of any committee or floor action.

industries.note: The bill would have ended key tactics for extending market exclusivity: late patent listing, repeated 30-month stays on new patents, and late infringement suits. Its industry interest ran against consumers, who pay brand-name prices when generic entry is delayed [S2].

The bill would have sped generic approvals and cleared blockers to entry, while disciplining first filers who sit on their 180-day exclusivity. Cheaper generics pass savings to patients, so the industry's gain ran alongside the public's [S2].
